Package frc.robot.subsystems.arm

Class AbstractArmSubsystem

java.lang.Object
edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.SubsystemBase
frc.robot.subsystems.SubsystemBase
frc.robot.subsystems.arm.AbstractArmSubsystem
All Implemented Interfaces:
edu.wpi.first.util.sendable.Sendable, edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.Subsystem, Subsystem, AutoCloseable
Direct Known Subclasses:
ArmSubsystem, SimArmSubsystem
public abstract class AbstractArmSubsystem extends SubsystemBase
The public API for an arm, and the control logic shared by its implementations.

This is the class robot code should hold. It exposes the two things a caller can ask of an arm — go to an angle, or stop driving — and nothing else. How those requests reach a motor is left to the subclass: ArmSubsystem drives real hardware and SimArmSubsystem advances a physics model. A caller holding this type cannot tell which it has.

Position control only. An arm here always holds an angle. There is no velocity mode and no mode enum, because a mode field that only ever holds one value is a state nothing can be in and a branch nothing can take.

What this class deliberately does not expose

  • Voltage control. Useful for characterising a mechanism in a test, dangerous in match code, and unnecessary for anything a robot actually does. Subclasses have voltage-level access through their hooks; this API does not.
  • PID gains. Tuning is a property of the hardware, so it belongs to the hardware subclass. Exposing it here would invite per-loop retuning.
  • Encoder zeroing and calibration. A calibration routine is a sequence of moves and waits, which is command logic. The API exposes getAngle() and isAtLowerLimit() for such a routine to be built on.
  • Raw sensors. The named accessors (getAngle(), getVelocity(), isAtLowerLimit()) are the whole read surface; robot logic should use them rather than reaching into a subclass's own fields.

Subclassing

Three kinds of class extend this, and each has a different job:

  • ArmSubsystem — the real mechanism. Wire the motor in its constructor, then implement the four hooks below to read the encoder, close the loop, and command the motor.
  • SimArmSubsystem — the simulated mechanism, driving a WPILib SingleJointedArmSim.
  • A team's own subclass — a robot-specific mechanism, or a variant over a vendor motor controller. Override the hooks and add behaviour such as a scoring angle.

The loop, and the hooks a subclass implements

SubsystemBase.periodic() runs, in order:

  1. sample() — refresh the mechanism's own sensor values.
  2. holdAngle(Angle) or releaseOutput() — command it.
  3. the goal flag is updated from the freshly sampled values.

The ordering is what keeps the goal flag consistent with the values the decision was made from. It also means an applied voltage becomes visible on the next loop, which is how a real motor controller behaves.

  • Method Details

    • setTargetAngle

      public void setTargetAngle(edu.wpi.first.units.measure.Angle angle)
      Commands the arm to move to and hold an angle.

      The target is clamped to the mechanism's travel range, so an out-of-range request moves to the nearest legal angle instead of being rejected. That is what a driver wants mid-match; callers that need to detect the condition should check isAngleAllowed(Angle) first.

      Safe to call from any thread, and safe to call every loop — repeating the same target is cheap and does not disturb the mechanism.

      Parameters:
      angle - the target angle, measured from the zero position

    • setIdle

      public void setIdle()
      Commands the arm to stop moving and drop its output.

      The last target is remembered, so calling setTargetAngle(Angle) again resumes control immediately. Whether the arm then holds or sags is the mechanism's brake mode.

    • zeroPosition

      public void zeroPosition()
      Defines the current joint angle as the zero reference.

      Call this with the arm resting on its lower hard stop. Until it runs, angles are measured from wherever the encoder powered up, so absolute targets are meaningless.

    • getLastAppliedVolts

      public double getLastAppliedVolts()
      Returns the voltage applied to the motor last loop.

      Reported from the motor controller, so it reflects what the hardware actually did rather than what was requested. On the loop a command is first issued this still reads the previous loop's value, which is how a real controller behaves.

      Returns:
      the applied voltage in volts

    • periodicImpl

      protected final void periodicImpl()
      Samples the mechanism, applies the current command, and updates the goal flag.

      Declared final: the ordering here is what keeps the goal flag consistent with the values the decision was made from. Subclasses supply behaviour through the hooks below rather than by overriding this. For extra work that must not hold the state lock, override SubsystemBase.beforePeriodic() or SubsystemBase.afterPeriodic().

      Specified by:
      periodicImpl in class SubsystemBase

    • sample

      protected void sample()
      Refreshes the mechanism's sensor values.

      Called once per loop, before any command is issued. Implementations should read their encoder and limit switches here, so that getAngle(), isAtLowerLimit(), and the rest report values from this loop.

      The default implementation does nothing, which is correct for a mechanism whose sensors are read on demand and for a test double that holds its values in fields.

    • sampleAngle

      protected abstract edu.wpi.first.units.measure.Angle sampleAngle()
      Returns the arm's current joint angle.

      Implementations supply this from their own sensor — an encoder for hardware, the plant for a simulation. The shared layer calls it rather than caching a value, so a logger or a test always sees the live reading.

      Returns:
      the current joint angle

    • holdAngle

      protected abstract void holdAngle(edu.wpi.first.units.measure.Angle angle)
      Drives the arm to hold angle.

      Called once per loop while the mechanism is enabled. Implementations close the loop however suits their hardware: a vendor motor controller's onboard position control, or a WPILib PIDController plus feedforward, as ArmSubsystem and SimArmSubsystem both do.

      angle is already clamped to the travel range, so implementations need not re-validate it.

      Parameters:
      angle - the angle to hold, measured from the zero position

    • driveOpenLoop

      protected abstract void driveOpenLoop(double velocityRotationsPerSecond)
      Drives the arm open-loop at a velocity.

      Not reached from any command in this API; it exists so a subclass can build a calibration routine — drive into the lower stop until isAtLowerLimit() trips, then zeroPosition() — without reaching around the abstraction for raw voltage.

      Parameters:
      velocityRotationsPerSecond - the velocity to drive at, positive raising the arm

    • releaseOutput

      protected abstract void releaseOutput()
      Stops commanding the mechanism.

      Called while idle and on SubsystemBase.stop(). Whether the arm then holds or sags is the hardware's brake mode, not a decision this method makes.

    • zeroEncoder

      protected abstract void zeroEncoder()
      Defines the current angle as the zero reference.

      Called by zeroPosition(). Implementations should reset both the sensor and any internal setpoint.
